prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: I ranked B014 first in the opening, but after reading colleagues' maturity arguments I now prefer B022 as the lead proposal. The China-shock and task-based work addresses a first-order question: how trade and technology change who earns what, and where. The evidence is also unusually transparent. Designs are explicit, data are widely available, and the main results have been replicated, re-analysed and contested for roughly a decade, with the contested parts (magnitudes, persistence, mechanisms) in the open. As a metascience-minded member, I weight that record of scrutiny heavily. A finding that has survived critique is a stronger basis for a prize than one whose causal reading is still being established. The programme also has wide policy influence and fits across labour, trade and public economics. Attribution is cleanest with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. They jointly produced the trade-shock papers, and Autor and Dorn also co-authored the polarisation work, so one citation can name both trade and technology channels.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification and durability. Shift-share designs are sensitive to critique, and estimates of the size and persistence of the China-shock effects have been qualified. The task framework has important contributors outside this credited set (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane), and Acemoglu was recognised in 2024 for related themes, so the citation must be narrow and honest about what the prize names. Lawrence Katz has a real claim to the earlier skill-premium literature, and a three-person limit forces an exclusion that is contestable. I also see B014 as a possibly stronger discovery in the long run, but it is younger.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B022 fifth and proposes only Autor and Hanson. He argues the 2024 prize overlaps thematically, and that the persistent-effects findings have been challenged in re-analyses. He ranks B014 seventh as less mature, with causal place effects still under scrutiny.
responses.response: I agree on B014's relative youth. That is a main reason I have moved it from first to alternative. I partly agree that the persistence findings have been qualified, but the qualifications argue for a carefully worded citation, not for dropping the work. I would keep Dorn. He is a full co-author of the China-shock papers and of the polarisation work with Autor, so a two-person prize would understate the joint design. On the 2024 overlap, I think the empirical trade-shock evidence is distinct from the institutions and growth contribution that was recognised.

responses.point: Andersson proposes Autor, Hanson and Katz for B022. He treats Katz as central to the skill-premium and technology-race literature, and Dorn as a defensible alternative. He notes that the replications and critiques of the China-shock magnitudes are ongoing.
responses.response: Katz's claim is real, but it rests mainly on the earlier education-technology race work, which is a different discovery from the trade-shock evidence and the tasks and polarisation papers. If the citation is about import competition and technological change shaping local labour demand, Dorn is the better third name. If the Committee wanted to honour the skill-premium strand, that would be a different and wider citation. I would first want to know whether it could be framed without leaving out the tasks and trade-shock authors. I agree with Andersson that the ongoing critiques of magnitudes belong in the discussion. I read them as a sign the work has been scrutinised, not as a reason to wait.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B014 first, as I did. She sees the combination of new administrative data and quasi-experimental design as a close fit to the data-discovery standard, notes replication across countries, and ranks B022 second.
responses.response: I share her view of B014's quality, and my own first-place ranking reflected it. The disagreement is about timing and robustness, not merit. The core mobility and place-effect results are mostly from 2014 to 2022, and some of the causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects is still being tested. B022 has had longer to be stress-tested. If the Committee accepts a younger prize, B014 remains my first alternative, with Chetty, Hendren and Friedman. I would not want it to be treated as a data-and-measurement prize alone, so the citation would need to name the causal findings.

uncertainties: How much the shift-share identification critiques and the persistence debates should qualify the China-shock evidence in the citation.
Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name, which depends on how widely the citation is framed.
How the Committee weighs the thematic proximity of the 2024 prize on technology and institutions.
Whether B014's causal neighbourhood-effect evidence will be seen as mature enough to take precedence over B022.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B022 or the listed alternatives. My frequent co-authors and networks (Camerer, Brodeur, Johannesson, Rand, Nowak and others) do not appear among the credited names on those ballots. Stockholm affiliation is relevant only to B047, which I do not propose.
